pay_source: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Occupational Employment and Wage Statistics, May 2025 (Georgia and national), via O*NET OnLine. Starting = 10th percentile, typical = median.

trades.name: Electrician
trades.summary: Install and repair wiring, lighting and power in homes, businesses and factories.
trades.work: You read plans, run wire and conduit, connect panels and outlets, and find and fix problems safely. Indoors and outdoors, on your feet, with a lot of problem solving.
trades.outlook: Georgia jobs expected to grow 15% from 2024 to 2034, about 2,340 openings a year.

paths.label: Electrical Systems Technology diploma or Electrical Technician certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant; pay fees and tools

paths.label: IBEW/NECA inside wireman apprenticeship (union electrical training)
paths.cost: Little or no tuition; you earn while you learn
paths.note: Needs one year of algebra with a passing grade and an aptitude test.

paths.label: Non-union employer apprenticeship (for example through a contractor or Apprentice Georgia)
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: Georgia licenses electrical contractors, not workers: you work under a licensed contractor. To get your own Class I or II contractor license you need to be 21, have 4 years of experience and pass an exam.
license.other_states: Most other states license journeyman electricians statewide, so you may need a state exam if you move.

trades.name: Lineworker (power lines)
trades.summary: Build and repair the power lines that bring electricity to homes and towns.
trades.work: You climb poles and work from bucket trucks, often outdoors in all weather, and help restore power after storms. Physical, team-based work with strong pay.

paths.label: Electrical Lineworker certificate at a Georgia technical college
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Southeast Lineman Training Center, Trenton, Georgia
paths.cost: $24,555 including Class A CDL training
paths.note: No dorms; the school helps find local housing. Classes start January, May and September.

paths.label: Utility or electric co-op lineworker apprenticeship after school
paths.cost: Paid job

license.georgia: No state license. Most employers want a Class A commercial driver's license (CDL).

trades.name: Plumber or pipefitter
trades.summary: Install and fix water, gas and drain pipes in homes, buildings and plants.
trades.work: You read plans, cut and join pipe, install fixtures and water heaters, and track down leaks. Pipefitters build high-pressure systems in factories and power plants.

paths.label: NCCER Plumbing and Pipefitting Technology diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: UA plumbers and pipefitters apprenticeship (for example Local 72 in Atlanta)
paths.cost: $60 application fee at Local 72; classes covered

paths.label: Employer apprenticeship with a plumbing company
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: Georgia has a state Journeyman Plumber license: 1 year of plumbing work, three references and an exam. Master Plumber needs 5 years, 2 of them as a licensed journeyman, and an exam.
license.other_states: Nearly every state licenses plumbers, with its own exam.

finders.label: Find a UA local (plumbers and pipefitters)

trades.name: HVAC technician (heating and air)
trades.summary: Install and repair heating, air conditioning and refrigeration systems.
trades.work: You visit homes and businesses, test and fix systems, and handle refrigerants safely. Busy year-round in Georgia's heat.

paths.label: Air Conditioning Technology diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Employer or union (UA, SMART) apprenticeship
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: Federal EPA Section 608 certification is required to handle refrigerants (no minimum age). To run your own business, Georgia's Conditioned Air Contractor license needs 4 to 5 years of experience, EPA certification, a design course and an exam.

trades.name: Welder
trades.summary: Join metal parts for buildings, ships, pipelines, cars and machines.
trades.work: You use different welding methods (stick, MIG, TIG), read blueprints and pass welding tests. Work is in shops, factories, shipyards and job sites.

paths.label: Welding and Joining Technology diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Pipe welding through UA, Ironworkers or Boilermakers apprenticeships
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

license.georgia: No license. Employers want American Welding Society (AWS) certifications, which are welding tests you take.

trades.name: CNC machine operator
trades.summary: Run computer-controlled machines that cut metal and plastic parts. The fastest way into machining.
trades.work: You load material, start the program, watch the machine run and measure finished parts to make sure they are right. Many people start here and move up to setup, machinist or programmer.
trades.outlook: Georgia jobs expected to stay about the same from 2024 to 2034, about 200 openings a year.

paths.label: CNC Specialist or Machine Tool certificate at a technical college
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant (Precision Manufacturing)

paths.label: Hired as an entry-level operator and trained on the job
paths.length: A few weeks to a few months, paid
paths.cost: Free; many plants hire right out of high school
paths.note: A certificate or NIMS credential helps you get hired and paid more.

paths.label: Dual enrollment: start CNC classes in high school
paths.cost: Free in Georgia through Dual Enrollment

license.georgia: No license. NIMS (National Institute for Metalworking Skills) credentials are tests that show employers you can measure and run machines safely.

finders.label: NIMS machining credentials and test sites

trades.name: CNC machinist
trades.summary: Set up and run lathes and mills to make precise metal parts, from the drawing to the finished piece.
trades.work: You read drawings, pick tools, set up lathes and mills, adjust programs and measure parts to thousandths of an inch. More skill than an operator, and more pay.
trades.outlook: Georgia jobs expected to grow 10% from 2024 to 2034, about 760 openings a year.

paths.label: CNC Technology or Precision Machining and Manufacturing diploma
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Manufacturer machinist apprenticeship
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: No license. NIMS credentials are optional and valued by employers.

finders.label: NIMS machining credentials and test sites

trades.name: CNC programmer
trades.summary: Write the computer programs that tell CNC machines how to cut each part. The top-paid job in machining.
trades.work: You turn 3D drawings into machine programs with CAD/CAM software, choose tools and speeds, test new programs and fix problems. Mostly at a computer, close to the shop floor.
trades.outlook: Georgia jobs expected to grow 25% from 2024 to 2034, about 40 openings a year. Most programmers start as machinists.

paths.label: Precision Machining and Manufacturing associate degree, or CNC Technology diploma plus CAD/CAM classes
paths.cost: Diploma tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant; degrees can use the HOPE Scholarship or Pell

paths.label: Move up from machinist after a few years on the job
paths.cost: Paid; employers often pay for CAM software classes

license.georgia: No license. NIMS CNC programming credentials and CAM software certificates help you move up.

finders.label: NIMS machining credentials and test sites

trades.name: Tool and die maker
trades.summary: Build the molds, dies and special tools that factories use to make parts in the thousands.
trades.work: An advanced machinist job: you use CNC and manual machines, grinders and measuring tools to build tooling that must be exact. Often reached through a long apprenticeship.

paths.label: Tool and die maker apprenticeship with a manufacturer
paths.cost: Usually free to you

paths.label: Precision Machining and Manufacturing diploma or degree, then on-the-job training
paths.length: 1 to 2 years of school, then work experience
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license. NIMS credentials and a finished apprenticeship are what employers look for.

finders.label: NIMS machining credentials and test sites

trades.name: Industrial maintenance and mechatronics technician
trades.summary: Keep factory machines, robots and production lines running.
trades.work: You troubleshoot electrical, mechanical and computer controls, fix breakdowns and do planned maintenance. Georgia's plants hire these techs constantly.

paths.label: Industrial Systems Technology or Mechatronics diploma, or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Manufacturer apprenticeship
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Automotive technician
trades.summary: Diagnose and repair cars and light trucks, including hybrids and electric vehicles.
trades.work: You use computer scanners and hand tools to find problems, then fix engines, brakes, steering, electrical systems and more.
trades.outlook: US jobs expected to grow 5 to 6% from 2025 to 2035.

paths.label: Automotive Technology diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Dealer or manufacturer training programs
paths.cost: Varies; some are paid

license.georgia: No license. ASE certifications are optional and raise pay; refrigerant work needs EPA 609.

trades.name: Diesel technician
trades.summary: Repair the big engines in trucks, buses, tractors and generators.
trades.work: You diagnose and rebuild diesel engines, brakes and electronics on heavy vehicles. Strong demand from trucking and logistics around Georgia's ports and highways.

paths.label: Diesel Equipment Technology diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Dealer or fleet apprenticeship
paths.cost: Usually free to you

license.georgia: No license. ASE certifications help; some jobs want a CDL to road-test trucks.

trades.name: Heavy equipment mechanic
trades.summary: Fix bulldozers, cranes, excavators and farm and mining machines.
trades.work: Hydraulics, engines and electronics on huge machines, in shops or out at job sites.

paths.label: Diesel or heavy equipment program at a technical college
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia when the program is on the HOPE Career Grant list

paths.label: Dealer technician programs (for example equipment makers' dealer networks)
paths.cost: Varies

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Auto body and collision repair
trades.summary: Repair and repaint cars after accidents.
trades.work: You straighten frames, replace panels, match paint and make cars look new again. Part craft, part science.

paths.label: Auto Collision Repair diploma or certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license. I-CAR and ASE training are valued.

trades.name: Aircraft mechanic (A&P)
trades.summary: Inspect and repair airplanes and helicopters so they are safe to fly.
trades.work: You follow strict maintenance manuals on engines, landing gear and electronics. Atlanta's airport, Delta and aerospace plants hire many.

paths.label: Aviation Maintenance Technology at an FAA Part 147 school (several Georgia technical colleges)
paths.cost: Aviation Technology is on Georgia's HOPE Career Grant list; ask the college which programs qualify

paths.label: Military aircraft maintenance
paths.cost: Paid
paths.note: Military experience can count toward the FAA license.

license.georgia: Federal FAA Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) certificate: age 18, read and speak English, finish an FAA Part 147 school or get 18 to 30 months of experience, then pass written, oral and practical tests.

trades.name: Truck driver (CDL)
trades.summary: Drive tractor-trailers and haul goods across the state or the country.
trades.work: Long-haul drivers are away for days; local and regional drivers are home most nights. Georgia's ports and warehouses need many drivers.

paths.label: Commercial Truck Driving certificate at a Georgia technical college
paths.cost: HOPE Grant plus up to $1,100 HOPE Career Grant for the program

paths.label: Company-paid CDL training (you agree to drive for them for a time)
paths.cost: Paid by the company; read the contract

license.georgia: Commercial driver's license from Georgia DDS: age 18 to drive only inside Georgia, 21 to cross state lines or haul hazardous materials. You hold a learner's permit at least 14 days and finish federal entry-level driver training first.

trades.name: Heavy equipment operator
trades.summary: Run bulldozers, excavators and cranes on road and building projects.
trades.work: Outdoor work moving earth and materials with precision; projects change often.

paths.label: Operating Engineers (IUOE) apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

paths.label: Operator school
paths.cost: Varies; compare carefully

license.georgia: No state license for most equipment. Crane operators usually need national (NCCCO) certification.

trades.name: Carpenter
trades.summary: Build frames, floors, stairs and cabinets for homes and buildings.
trades.work: You measure, cut and assemble wood and other materials, from framing houses to finish work.

paths.label: Carpentry diploma or Framing Carpenter certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Carpenters union apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

paths.label: Learn on the job with a builder
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No license for workers. Running your own building company needs a Georgia residential or general contractor license.

trades.name: Brick and block mason
trades.summary: Build walls, chimneys and buildings with brick, block and stone.
trades.work: Outdoor, physical craft work where you can see what you built for decades.

paths.label: Bricklayers (BAC) apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

paths.label: Masonry program at some technical colleges
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Ironworker
trades.summary: Raise the steel frames of bridges, stadiums and tall buildings.
trades.work: You work at heights, bolt and weld steel beams and place rebar. Team work with strict safety.

pay.note: Pay is much higher in some other states.

paths.label: Ironworkers apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Sheet metal worker
trades.summary: Make and install ducts, roofs, signs and metal parts for buildings.
trades.work: Shop and job-site work cutting, bending and joining metal, often on heating and air systems.

paths.label: SMART sheet metal apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Boilermaker
trades.summary: Build and repair boilers, tanks and vessels in power plants and refineries.
trades.work: Heavy welding and rigging on big industrial projects; often travel between job sites.

paths.label: Boilermakers union apprenticeship
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

license.georgia: No license.

trades.thin_in_georgia: Few jobs in Georgia. Most work is near power plants, refineries and shipyards in the Gulf Coast, Midwest and other industrial states, and boilermakers often travel.

trades.name: Elevator installer and repairer
trades.summary: Install and fix elevators, escalators and moving walkways.
trades.work: Electrical, mechanical and computer work inside elevator shafts and machine rooms. One of the best-paid trades.

pay.note: Georgia's starting figure is unreliable, so it is left out.

paths.label: Elevator constructors (IUEC) apprenticeship with NEIEP classes
paths.cost: Little or no tuition
paths.note: Openings are rare and competitive; mostly in big metro areas such as Atlanta.

license.georgia: Georgia rules for elevator mechanics are not confirmed yet; many other states require a state license.

trades.name: Construction manager
trades.summary: Run building projects: schedules, budgets, crews and safety.
trades.work: Part office, part job site. Many start in a trade, then move up; a degree helps.

paths.label: Construction Management diploma or certificates, or a two-year degree
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Work up from a trade or field engineer role
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No license to work as a manager. Owning a building company needs a Georgia residential or general contractor license.

trades.name: Solar panel installer
trades.summary: Put solar panels on roofs and in solar farms.
trades.work: Outdoor work on roofs and fields mounting panels and connecting them. Wiring hookups are done under an electrical contractor.

paths.label: Photovoltaic Systems Installation and Repair certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Learn on the job with a solar company
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No installer license. NABCEP certification is optional.

trades.name: Wind turbine technician
trades.summary: Climb and repair the giant turbines on wind farms.
trades.work: You climb hundreds of feet, fix gearboxes and electronics, and travel to wind farms.

pay.note: Georgia has too few jobs to report pay.

paths.label: Wind energy technology at community colleges in wind states (for example Iowa, Texas, New Mexico)
paths.cost: Out-of-state tuition unless you move there first

paths.label: Private wind technician programs
paths.cost: Varies

license.georgia: No license; climbing and safety certifications are required by employers.

trades.thin_in_georgia: Georgia has almost no wind farms. Jobs are mainly in Texas, the Plains (Iowa, Oklahoma, Kansas) and Illinois.

trades.name: Commercial diver
trades.summary: Work underwater building, welding and inspecting docks, pipelines and ships.
trades.work: Demanding and sometimes risky work, often offshore for weeks. Pairs well with welding skills.

pay.note: Georgia has too few jobs to report pay.

paths.label: Commercial Diving at South Louisiana Community College
paths.cost: Out-of-state tuition plus dive gear

paths.label: Private dive schools on the Gulf Coast, East Coast and in Seattle
paths.cost: Often $15,000 or more; check accreditation and federal aid

license.georgia: No state license. Employers expect an accredited commercial diving school certificate and a dive physical.

trades.thin_in_georgia: Most jobs are on the Gulf Coast (Louisiana, Texas) for offshore energy, plus big ports.

trades.name: Boat and small engine mechanic
trades.summary: Repair boat motors, outboards, lawn equipment and motorcycles.
trades.work: Hands-on engine work at marinas, dealers and repair shops; Georgia's coast and lakes have marinas.

paths.label: Small engine or marine technology program
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

paths.label: Marine technician schools (Florida and other coastal states)
paths.cost: Varies

license.georgia: No license; engine makers offer certifications.

trades.name: Farm equipment mechanic
trades.summary: Keep tractors, combines and irrigation equipment running on farms.
trades.work: Engines, hydraulics and GPS electronics, often out on farms. Big need in rural Georgia.

paths.label: Diesel or agricultural equipment program
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia when the program is on the HOPE Career Grant list

paths.label: Equipment dealer technician program
paths.cost: Varies

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Farrier (horseshoeing)
trades.summary: Trim horses' hooves and fit horseshoes.
trades.work: Physical, skilled work at barns and horse farms. Most farriers run their own business and build a client list.

pay.note: There is no federal pay data for farriers; income depends on how many horses you shoe.

paths.label: Farrier school (a few weeks to 6 months), then work alongside an experienced farrier
paths.length: Weeks to months, plus 1 to 2 years helping
paths.cost: Varies by school
paths.note: Only a few farrier schools exist nationwide, mostly outside Georgia.

license.georgia: No license. American Farrier's Association certification is voluntary.

trades.thin_in_georgia: Few farrier schools anywhere; expect to travel for training. Horse country (Kentucky, Texas, Florida, Oklahoma) has the most work.

trades.name: Veterinary technician
trades.summary: The nurse of the animal world: help vets with exams, surgery, X-rays and lab work.
trades.work: Hands-on care for pets, horses or farm animals in clinics and hospitals. A great step toward vet school too.

paths.label: Veterinary Technology associate degree (AVMA accredited)
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or HOPE Grant can help in Georgia

license.georgia: Registered veterinary technician through the Georgia State Board of Veterinary Medicine: finish an accredited program and pass the national VTNE exam.

trades.name: Landscaping and turf care
trades.summary: Design, plant and care for lawns, golf courses, parks and gardens.
trades.work: Outdoor work with plants and equipment; can grow into running your own business or managing a golf course.

paths.label: Horticulture or turfgrass program
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

paths.label: Learn on the job
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No license for general work. Spraying pesticides for pay needs a Georgia Department of Agriculture applicator license.

trades.name: Water and wastewater plant operator
trades.summary: Run the plants that clean drinking water and wastewater for towns.
trades.work: You watch gauges and computer controls, test water and keep pumps running. Steady government jobs.

paths.label: Hired as a trainee by a city or county, with short courses
paths.cost: Often paid by the employer

license.georgia: Georgia operator certificates rise by class with experience and exams (State Board of Examiners for water and wastewater operators).

trades.name: Licensed practical nurse (LPN)
trades.summary: Care for patients in nursing homes, clinics and hospitals under RNs and doctors.
trades.work: You check vital signs, give medicines, change bandages and help patients day to day. A fast start that can lead to an RN degree later.

paths.label: Practical Nursing diploma
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant
paths.note: Extra entrance testing and health records are required.

license.georgia: Georgia Board of Nursing license after passing the NCLEX-PN exam.

trades.name: Certified nursing assistant (CNA)
trades.summary: Help patients bathe, eat and move, and keep nurses informed.
trades.work: Caring, hands-on work in nursing homes and hospitals. The quickest way into health care, often while studying nursing.

paths.label: Nurse Aide certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Training paid by a nursing home
paths.cost: Often free

license.georgia: Listed on the Georgia nurse aide registry after an approved training program and a written and skills test.

trades.name: Medical assistant
trades.summary: Help in doctors' offices with patients, blood draws and paperwork.
trades.work: A mix of patient care and office work in clinics; regular daytime hours.

paths.label: Medical Assisting diploma
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No Georgia license. National certification (CMA or RMA) is valued.

trades.name: Dental hygienist
trades.summary: Clean teeth, take X-rays and teach patients to care for their teeth.
trades.work: One-on-one patient care in dental offices with regular hours and high pay for a two-year degree.

paths.label: Dental Hygiene associate degree (CODA accredited)
paths.length: About 2 to 3 years including required classes
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship can help in Georgia
paths.note: Competitive entry with science prerequisites.

license.georgia: Georgia Board of Dentistry license after an accredited program, the national board exam and a clinical exam.

trades.name: Surgical technologist
trades.summary: Prepare operating rooms and hand instruments to surgeons.
trades.work: Fast-paced, precise teamwork in the operating room.

paths.label: Surgical Technology diploma or associate degree
paths.cost: HOPE Grant or Scholarship in Georgia

license.georgia: No Georgia license. Employers want the national CST certification.

trades.name: Radiologic (X-ray) technologist
trades.summary: Take X-rays and other medical images that help doctors find problems.
trades.work: Patient care plus imaging machines; can move up to CT and MRI.

paths.label: Radiologic Technology associate degree
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship can help in Georgia
paths.note: Competitive entry.

license.georgia: Employers require national ARRT certification; check Georgia's current state rules.

trades.name: EMT and paramedic
trades.summary: Answer 911 calls and give emergency care on the way to the hospital.
trades.work: Shift work on ambulances; you make fast decisions under pressure. EMT comes first, paramedic is the advanced level.

paths.label: EMT certificate, then Paramedicine diploma
paths.length: EMT about 1 semester; paramedic 1 to 2 years more
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: State EMS license from the Georgia Department of Public Health after an approved course and the national NREMT exam. Age 18.

trades.name: Pharmacy technician
trades.summary: Help pharmacists fill prescriptions and serve customers.
trades.work: Careful, detail work in drugstores and hospitals.

paths.label: Pharmacy Technology certificate or diploma
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

paths.label: Drugstore training programs
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: Register with the Georgia Board of Pharmacy. Many employers want national certification (PTCB).

trades.name: Cosmetologist and hair designer
trades.summary: Cut, color and style hair, and do skin and nail care.
trades.work: Creative, people-focused work in salons; many cosmetologists build their own clients or open a salon.

pay.note: Tips and your own client list can raise income a lot.

paths.label: Cosmetology diploma at a technical college
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia; far cheaper than most private beauty schools

paths.label: Private beauty school
paths.cost: Often $10,000 to $20,000; compare carefully

paths.label: Apprenticeship in a licensed salon
paths.cost: Low

license.georgia: Georgia State Board of Cosmetology and Barbers: age 17, high school diploma or GED, 1,500 school hours (or 3,000 apprenticeship hours), then written and practical exams. Hair designer: 1,325 hours.
license.other_states: Required hours range from about 1,000 to 2,100 by state.

trades.name: Barber
trades.summary: Cut and style hair and shave and trim beards.
trades.work: Social work in barbershops; many barbers rent a chair or own the shop.

pay.note: Tips and a loyal client list raise income.

paths.label: Barbering diploma
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

paths.label: Apprenticeship under a licensed master barber
paths.cost: Low

license.georgia: Georgia State Board of Cosmetology and Barbers license after approved training and state exams.

trades.name: Nail technician and esthetician
trades.summary: Do manicures, nail art, facials and skin care.
trades.work: Detailed, creative work with clients in salons and spas.

paths.label: Nail Technician or Esthetician certificate
paths.length: Nails 525 hours (4+ months); esthetics 1,000 hours (9+ months)
paths.cost: HOPE Grant in Georgia

license.georgia: Georgia board license: age 17, high school diploma or GED, 525 hours for nails or 1,000 hours for esthetics, then exams.

trades.name: Police officer or sheriff's deputy
trades.summary: Protect the community, respond to calls and enforce the law.
trades.work: Shift work patrolling, investigating and helping people; physical and mental tests to get in.

paths.label: Basic Law Enforcement certificate at a technical college or an agency academy
paths.cost: HOPE Grant plus up to $3,750 HOPE Career Grant in Georgia; agencies often pay recruits

license.georgia: Certified by Georgia POST after the academy and state exam. Many agencies hire at 21.

trades.name: Firefighter
trades.summary: Fight fires and answer medical emergencies.
trades.work: 24-hour shifts at a station, training, and emergency calls. Most departments want EMT certification too.

paths.label: Fire academy after being hired by a department, plus EMT
paths.cost: Usually paid by the department

license.georgia: Basic Firefighter certification through the Georgia Firefighter Standards and Training Council. Age 18.

trades.name: IT support and help desk
trades.summary: Fix computers, accounts and networks for people at work.
trades.work: You solve tech problems in person and over the phone; a common first step into networking and cybersecurity.

paths.label: Help Desk Specialist or CompTIA A+ certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license. CompTIA A+ is the usual first certification.

trades.name: Network technician
trades.summary: Set up and maintain the networks and Wi-Fi that businesses run on.
trades.work: Install routers and switches, watch network health and fix outages.

paths.label: Networking Specialist diploma or Cisco certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license. Network+ and Cisco CCNA are common.

trades.name: Cybersecurity technician
trades.summary: Protect computers and networks from hackers.
trades.work: Watch for attacks, fix weak spots and respond to incidents. Top pay usually comes after a few years of IT experience.

pay.note: These figures are for experienced information security analysts; first jobs often start in IT support.

paths.label: Cybersecurity diploma or certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license. CompTIA Security+ is the usual starting certification.

trades.name: Commercial drone pilot
trades.summary: Fly drones for photos, surveys, farms, inspections and film.
trades.work: Often a skill added to another job (real estate, farming, construction, film) or a small business.

pay.note: No federal pay data; income depends on the work.

paths.label: Small Unmanned Aircraft (drone) certificate
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: Federal FAA Part 107 remote pilot certificate: age 16, pass the knowledge test and a security check.

trades.name: Cook and chef
trades.summary: Cook in restaurants, hotels, hospitals and catering, and lead a kitchen.
trades.work: Fast-paced kitchen work, nights and weekends; head chefs plan menus and run the crew.

pay.note: Chefs and head cooks. Line cooks: $35,940 typical in Georgia.

paths.label: Culinary Arts diploma or degree
paths.cost: HOPE Grant or Scholarship in Georgia

paths.label: Work up from line cook
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No license; a food safety certificate (ServSafe) is common.

trades.name: Film and TV set crew
trades.summary: Build sets, run lights and rigging, or do hair and makeup on film and TV productions.
trades.work: Long days on set, project to project. Georgia is one of the biggest filming states in the country.

pay.note: Pay is by the day or week and depends on the job and union status.

paths.label: Georgia Film Academy certificates at technical colleges (on-set production, grip and rigging, lighting, scenic, hair and makeup)
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

license.georgia: No license.

trades.name: Logistics and warehouse technician
trades.summary: Move goods through warehouses, ports and distribution centers.
trades.work: Run forklifts and scanners, manage inventory and shipping; can move up to logistics management.

paths.label: Logistics Management certificates
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant

paths.label: Hired and trained by a warehouse
paths.cost: Paid

license.georgia: No license; forklift certification is done by the employer.

trades.name: Millwright
trades.summary: Move, install and fix big factory machines, from conveyor lines to turbines.
trades.work: You read plans, take apart and rebuild heavy machinery, line it up to tiny tolerances and keep plants running. Factories, power plants and paper mills hire millwrights.

paths.label: Millwright apprenticeship through the carpenters' union
paths.cost: Little or no tuition; you earn while you learn

paths.label: Industrial Systems Technology or Industrial Maintenance diploma
paths.cost: Tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant (Industrial Maintenance)

license.georgia: No license. A finished apprenticeship and safety cards (like OSHA 10) are what employers look for.

trades.name: Power plant operator
trades.summary: Run the controls that make electricity at power plants. One of the best-paid jobs you can get without a degree.
trades.work: You watch gauges and computer screens, start and stop equipment, and keep the plant safe, often in 12-hour shifts. Georgia has coal, gas, solar and nuclear plants.

paths.label: Hired by an electric utility as a trainee operator
paths.cost: Free; you are paid while you train
paths.note: Utilities give a hiring test. Math, science and mechanical classes help.

paths.label: Energy, Electrical or Industrial Systems Technology at a technical college, then apply to utilities
paths.cost: Diploma tuition covered in Georgia with HOPE Grant + HOPE Career Grant (Industrial Maintenance)

paths.label: Navy nuclear or power plant jobs
paths.cost: Paid
paths.note: Navy reactor operators are hired by power companies after they serve.

license.georgia: No state license. Nuclear plant operators need a federal Nuclear Regulatory Commission license, which the employer trains you for. Power grid control-room operators need a NERC certificate.

trades.name: Substation and relay technician
trades.summary: Test and repair the equipment at substations and power plants that keeps the lights on.
trades.work: You work on transformers, breakers and protective relays, read wiring diagrams and use test equipment. Utilities like Georgia Power and electric co-ops hire these technicians.

paths.label: Utility apprenticeship (substation or relay technician)
paths.cost: Usually free to you

paths.label: Electronics or Electrical Engineering Technology associate degree, then hired by a utility
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help

license.georgia: No license. Employers train you and may want NETA test technician certification later.

trades.name: Avionics technician
trades.summary: Install and fix the electronics in airplanes: radios, navigation, autopilot and flight screens.
trades.work: Like an aircraft mechanic, but focused on wiring and computers. Atlanta's airport, airlines and aerospace plants in Savannah and Macon hire avionics techs.

paths.label: Avionics or Aviation Maintenance Technology program at a technical college
paths.cost: Aviation Technology is on Georgia's HOPE Career Grant list; ask the college which programs qualify

paths.label: Military avionics training
paths.cost: Paid
paths.note: Military experience counts with airlines and aerospace companies.

license.georgia: No state license. Many employers want the FAA Airframe and Powerplant (A&P) certificate or an FCC radio license.

trades.name: Crane operator
trades.summary: Lift steel, machines and shipping containers with giant cranes at job sites and ports.
trades.work: You run tower, mobile or port cranes, follow signals and plan every lift so it is safe. The Port of Savannah and big building projects hire crane operators.

paths.label: Operating engineers' union apprenticeship (IUOE)
paths.cost: Little or no tuition

paths.label: Crane operator school with NCCCO test prep
paths.cost: Several thousand dollars; check that the school is accredited

paths.label: Start as a rigger or oiler and move up
paths.cost: Free

license.georgia: Federal OSHA rules require construction crane operators to be certified, usually through NCCCO written and practical tests.

trades.name: Telecom and fiber line installer
trades.summary: Put up and fix the cables that bring internet, phone and TV to homes and businesses.
trades.work: You climb poles, use bucket trucks, bury cable and splice fiber-optic lines. Lots of work right now as fiber internet spreads to rural areas.

paths.label: Hired by a phone, cable or fiber company and trained on the job
paths.length: A few months to 1 year, paid
paths.cost: Free

paths.label: Telecommunications or Fiber Optics certificate at a technical college
paths.cost: Pell or HOPE Grant can help

license.georgia: No license. A driver's license and fiber optic certificates (like FOA) help you get hired.

trades.name: Air traffic controller
trades.summary: Guide airplanes safely in the air and on the ground. Very high pay, and no four-year degree is required.
trades.work: You watch radar and talk with pilots to keep planes apart, often at busy airports like Atlanta's. Fast thinking and staying calm matter most. Shift work, nights and weekends.

pay.note: Pay grows as you are certified at busier airports.

paths.label: Apply to the FAA when it opens hiring, then train at the FAA Academy in Oklahoma City
paths.length: Several months at the academy, then 2 to 3 years of paid training at your airport
paths.cost: Free; you are paid while you train
paths.note: Apply before age 31. You need to be a U.S. citizen, pass the FAA's skills test, a medical exam and a background check, and have college or work experience the FAA accepts.

paths.label: Military air traffic control
paths.cost: Paid
paths.note: Military controllers can be hired by the FAA later.

license.georgia: Federal: you are trained and certified by the FAA. No state license.

trades.name: Railroad conductor
trades.summary: Run freight trains and the crews on them. Railroads hire without a degree and pay you while you train.
trades.work: You check the train, couple and uncouple cars, and work with the engineer to move freight safely. Often on call, with time away from home. Many conductors later become engineers.

pay.note: Locomotive engineers: $81,410 typical in the US.

paths.label: Hired as a conductor trainee by a freight railroad (CSX and Norfolk Southern both run trains across Georgia)
paths.length: About 3 to 6 months of paid training
paths.cost: Free
paths.note: You need to be 18 or older with a high school diploma or GED, and pass a drug test and background check.

paths.label: Railroad operations certificate at a community college
paths.cost: Pell may help; check which railroads accept it

license.georgia: Federal Railroad Administration (FRA) conductor certification, which the railroad gives you during training.

trades.name: Boat captain and ship's officer
trades.summary: Run tugboats, ferries, fishing and charter boats, or big ships at sea.
trades.work: You start as a deckhand or at a maritime academy, log time on the water and earn U.S. Coast Guard licenses. The ports of Savannah and Brunswick need tugboat and harbor crews.

paths.label: Start as a deckhand on a tug, ferry or charter boat and earn sea time
paths.cost: Free; you pay for Coast Guard courses

paths.label: State or federal maritime academy (four-year degree plus a Coast Guard license)
paths.cost: Varies; some states offer in-state rates

license.georgia: Federal U.S. Coast Guard Merchant Mariner Credential, plus a captain's license that needs sea time and tests.

trades.thin_in_georgia: Georgia has jobs at its ports, but many more are on the Gulf Coast, the Mississippi River system and in the Northeast.

trades.name: Ultrasound technician (sonographer)
trades.summary: Use ultrasound to take pictures inside the body, like checking on a baby before birth.
trades.work: You work one-on-one with patients, move the ultrasound wand and capture clear images for doctors. Hospitals and clinics all over Georgia hire sonographers.

paths.label: Diagnostic Medical Sonography associate degree (look for CAAHEP accreditation)
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help
paths.note: Competitive entry.

license.georgia: No Georgia license, but employers require national certification from ARDMS (or ARRT) after you finish school.

trades.name: MRI technologist
trades.summary: Run MRI scanners that make detailed pictures of the brain, joints and organs.
trades.work: You prepare patients, keep them safe around the strong magnet and set up the scans. Many start as X-ray techs and add MRI, and some programs teach MRI from the start.

paths.label: Radiologic Technology associate degree, then an MRI certificate
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help
paths.note: Competitive entry.

license.georgia: No Georgia license, but employers require national ARRT certification in MRI.

trades.name: Physical therapist assistant
trades.summary: Help people get moving again after injuries, surgery or strokes.
trades.work: You lead patients through exercises a physical therapist plans, track their progress and cheer them on. Active work in clinics, hospitals, schools and sports medicine.

paths.label: Physical Therapist Assistant associate degree (CAPTE-accredited)
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help
paths.note: Competitive entry; watching or volunteering with a physical therapist helps.

license.georgia: Georgia license from the State Board of Physical Therapy after you pass the national PTA exam.

trades.name: Occupational therapy assistant
trades.summary: Help children and adults do everyday things again, like dressing, writing or cooking.
trades.work: You work under an occupational therapist with kids who have learning or motor delays, or adults after injuries or strokes. Schools, hospitals and rehab centers hire OTAs.

paths.label: Occupational Therapy Assistant associate degree (ACOTE-accredited)
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help
paths.note: Competitive entry.

license.georgia: Georgia license from the State Board of Occupational Therapy after you pass the national COTA exam.

trades.name: Respiratory therapist
trades.summary: Help people breathe: from newborn babies to patients on ventilators.
trades.work: You give breathing treatments, run ventilators in the ICU and respond to emergencies. Fast-paced hospital work with strong pay for a two-year degree.

paths.label: Respiratory Care associate degree (CoARC-accredited)
paths.cost: HOPE Scholarship or Pell can help
paths.note: Competitive entry.

license.georgia: Georgia license from the Georgia Composite Medical Board after you earn the national RRT or CRT credential.
license.other_states: Almost every state licenses respiratory therapists.

checklists.title: Apply to a technical or community college
checklists.summary: Open admission: most students who apply get in. These are the usual steps at Georgia's 22 technical colleges; other states' colleges are similar.

steps.title: Pick a college and program, and check its next start date
Fill out the college's online application and pay the fee ($25 in Georgia)
Send proof of residency and lawful presence (driver's license or ID)
Ask your school counselor to send your high school transcript (or send GED scores)
Send SAT or ACT scores, or take the ACCUPLACER placement test
File the FAFSA so you get Pell and state grants
Make sure the HOPE Grant (and HOPE Career Grant) show on your aid offer
Go to orientation, register for classes and buy tools or uniforms

checklists.title: Take a trade class in high school (Georgia Dual Enrollment)
checklists.summary: Free tuition, fees and books for up to 30 college hours. 10th graders can take career-tech classes; 11th and 12th graders can take any approved class.

steps.title: Talk to your school counselor about which trade classes fit your schedule
Apply to the technical college as a high school (dual enrollment) student
Fill out the Dual Enrollment funding application on GAfutures
Parent signs the Dual Enrollment participation agreement online
Counselor and college approve your courses

checklists.title: Apply for a union apprenticeship
checklists.summary: Paid on-the-job training plus classes. Apply to the local union or training center where you want to live and work, in any state.

steps.title: Find the local union or training center near where you want to work and note when applications open
Gather your transcript (showing a passing algebra grade), diploma or GED, driver's license and birth certificate
Practice algebra and reading for the aptitude test (no calculator allowed for electrical)
Submit the application and fee when the window is open
Take the aptitude test
Prepare for and go to the interview
Stay reachable while you are on the ranked list; update your phone and address

checklists.title: Find an employer apprenticeship
checklists.summary: Get hired by a company that trains you while you work. You are paid from day one.

steps.title: Search apprenticeship openings for this trade near you (and in other states if you are open to moving)
Ask the technical college's apprenticeship coordinator which employers are hiring
Update your resume with any shop classes, jobs and certifications
Apply to at least three employers
Follow up on each application and get ready for interviews

checklists.title: Get a commercial driver's license (CDL)
checklists.summary: 18 for driving inside one state, 21 to cross state lines.

steps.title: Pick a CDL program on the federal training provider registry (technical college or company school)
Pass a DOT medical exam
Pass the written tests and get your commercial learner's permit
Finish entry-level driver training (classroom and behind the wheel)
Take the skills (road) test at least 14 days after getting your permit

checklists.title: Start cosmetology, barbering or nail school
checklists.summary: Georgia requires set training hours, then state exams.

steps.title: Compare a technical college program with private schools: cost, hours and exam pass rates
Apply and send your diploma or GED (you must be at least 17)
File the FAFSA for Pell and the HOPE Grant
Buy your kit and uniform
Track your training hours toward the state requirement
Apply for the state board written and practical exams

checklists.title: Apply to a health care program
checklists.summary: Health programs add entrance tests, shots and a background check to the usual college steps, and some have waiting lists.

steps.title: Apply to the college and the program, and check its entry requirements and deadline
Take any required entrance test (for example the TEAS for nursing)
Get shot records, a physical and CPR certification
Complete the background check and drug screen
File the FAFSA for Pell and the HOPE Grant
Near the end of the program, register for the licensing or certification exam

checklists.title: Check out a private or specialty trade school
checklists.summary: Some trades are only taught at private schools. Check the facts before you sign.

steps.title: Check the school is accredited and accepts federal aid (search it on College Scorecard)
Ask for graduation and job placement rates and total cost including tools and housing
Compare with a public technical college or apprenticeship for the same trade
Apply for scholarships and file the FAFSA before signing anything
Apply and plan travel and housing

checklists.title: Train at a college in another state
checklists.summary: Out-of-state tuition is usually 2 to 4 times higher, and Georgia's HOPE money cannot be used outside Georgia.

steps.title: Compare out-of-state tuition with the in-state price and total living costs
Ask the college how to qualify for in-state tuition (often 12 months living there first)
Apply to the college and program
File the FAFSA: Pell Grants work in any state
Apply for trade scholarships that work anywhere (for example mikeroweWORKS)
Plan housing and travel

aid.name: Pell Grant
aid.summary: Federal grant money you don't pay back. Works at any eligible technical college, community college or trade school in any state, for programs of about 15 weeks or longer.
aid.who: Students with financial need, decided by the FAFSA. U.S. citizens and eligible noncitizens.
aid.apply: File the FAFSA each year. The school adds the Pell Grant to your aid offer.

aid.name: Workforce Pell Grant
aid.amount: Part of the Pell Grant, based on program length (up to $7,395 a year in 2026-27)
aid.summary: New from July 1, 2026: Pell money for short job-training programs of 8 to 15 weeks (150 to 599 clock hours), such as some CDL, welding and health certificates. Each program must be approved by the state and meet job-placement standards, so ask the school whether its program qualifies.
aid.who: Same rules as the Pell Grant. People who already have a bachelor's degree can still get it.
aid.apply: File the FAFSA and ask the school's financial aid office if your program is approved for Workforce Pell.

aid.name: Job training money from your local workforce office (WIOA)
aid.amount: Varies by area, often several thousand dollars toward training
aid.summary: Every state has American Job Centers that can pay for training in high-demand jobs through the federal Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act. In Georgia these are WorkSource Georgia offices.
aid.who: Adults 18 and older who qualify, people who lost a job, and young people 16 to 24 who are out of school. Rules and funding differ by area.
aid.apply: Find your nearest American Job Center, make an appointment and ask about training funds (an Individual Training Account).

aid.name: Registered and union apprenticeships
aid.amount: You earn a paycheck while you train, usually with raises as you learn
aid.summary: Apprenticeships combine a paid job with classes. Most have little or no tuition, so you finish without debt. They are open in every state.
aid.who: Usually 18 or older with a high school diploma or GED. Some trades also need algebra, an aptitude test or a driver's license.
aid.apply: Search Apprenticeship.gov and your local union training center, then follow each program's application dates.

aid.name: HOPE Grant
aid.amount: $107 per credit hour in 2026-27 (most of tuition)
aid.summary: Pays most of tuition for certificate and diploma programs at Georgia's 22 technical colleges. No high school GPA is needed to start.
aid.who: Georgia residents. Keep a 2.0 GPA at 30 and 60 hours to keep it.
aid.apply: File the FAFSA or Georgia's GSFAPP and enroll in an eligible program. It is added automatically.

aid.name: HOPE Career Grant
aid.amount: $500 a term at 9+ hours (more for some programs, such as truck driving)
aid.summary: Extra money on top of the HOPE Grant for high-demand programs like welding, electrical, HVAC, practical nursing, CDL and more. Together they make tuition free in those programs. You still pay fees, books and tools.
aid.who: Georgia residents who have the HOPE Grant and are in a program on the HOPE Career Grant list.
aid.apply: No extra form: it's added when you have the HOPE Grant and enroll in an eligible program.

aid.name: Zell Miller Grant
aid.amount: Full tuition for certificate and diploma programs
aid.summary: Replaces the HOPE Grant with full tuition for technical college students who keep a high college GPA.
aid.who: Georgia technical college students with a 3.5 college GPA.
aid.apply: Earn a 3.5 GPA in your program. Your college checks it at the end of each term.

aid.name: Dual Enrollment
aid.amount: Tuition, fees and books paid for up to 30 college hours
aid.summary: High school students take technical college classes for free and earn high school and college credit at the same time. Many students finish a welding, CNA or other certificate before graduating.
aid.who: Georgia students in 10th to 12th grade (10th graders can take career-tech classes).
aid.apply: Talk to your school counselor in the spring before the term, then apply to the technical college and fill in the Dual Enrollment form on GAfutures.

aid.name: Tennessee Promise
aid.amount: Tuition and fees not covered by other grants
aid.summary: Free tuition at Tennessee's community colleges and its 22+ Colleges of Applied Technology (TCATs), with a mentor.
aid.who: Tennessee high school seniors. Must file the FAFSA, go to a required meeting and do 8 to 16 hours of community service a year.
aid.apply: Apply online in the fall of senior year (the deadline is early November), then file the FAFSA.

aid.name: SC WINS
aid.amount: Up to $5,000 a year for what other aid leaves
aid.summary: Covers remaining tuition, fees and course costs at South Carolina's 16 technical colleges for high-demand programs.
aid.who: South Carolina residents in an eligible program who have a job, take a financial literacy course or do 100 volunteer hours. Keep a 2.0 GPA.
aid.apply: File the FAFSA and ask the technical college's financial aid office.

aid.name: Work Ready Kentucky Scholarship
aid.amount: Tuition for up to 60 credit hours
aid.summary: Tuition-free training in high-demand fields such as health care, manufacturing, construction and transportation in Kentucky.
aid.who: Kentucky residents with a high school diploma or working on a GED, who don't have an associate degree yet.
aid.apply: File the FAFSA and the Work Ready application through KHEAA (opens May 1 each year).

aid.name: Next NC Scholarship
aid.amount: At least $3,000 a year at a community college
aid.summary: Grant money for North Carolina community college and public university students from families earning $80,000 or less.
aid.who: North Carolina residents with family income of $80,000 or less and a FAFSA Student Aid Index of 7,500 or less.
aid.apply: Just file the FAFSA, by June 1 for the most money.

aid.name: Florida Bright Futures Gold Seal (Vocational and CAPE)
aid.amount: Set amount per credit hour at Florida schools
aid.summary: Florida's merit scholarship for career and technical programs. Gold Seal Vocational asks for career-tech grades and test scores; Gold Seal CAPE is for students who earn industry certifications in high school.
aid.who: Florida high school graduates who meet the grade, test or certification rules and 100 hours of service or paid work.
aid.apply: File the Florida Financial Aid Application by August 31 after high school graduation.

8.title: Take the trades interest quiz and read about three trades that fit you
Pick a career pathway for 9th grade (a set of three career classes; in Georgia these are CTAE pathways)

9.title: Take the first class in your career pathway
Join a career club such as SkillsUSA, FFA, HOSA or FCCLA
Find a summer job or helper role near the trade you like

10.title: Take the second class in your career pathway
Spend a day job-shadowing someone in a trade you like
Ask your counselor about Dual Enrollment: free technical college classes in high school

11.title: Finish your pathway and take its industry credential test if your school offers one
Ask your school about a youth apprenticeship or work-based learning (paid work for students 16 and up)
Visit a technical college, union training center or trade school, in your state or another
Save trade scholarships to apply for in senior year

12.title: Pick your trade and add its Steps to apply checklist
File the FAFSA for Pell, HOPE and other grants
Write down apprenticeship application dates for programs you like (many open only a few weeks a year)
